prompt.context: Our client is A+ Airline Co., the third largest airline in the United States by passengers carried. This week, we have been flying on our primary competitor, Gamma Airline, and we noticed something interesting: they stopped accepting cash for in-flight food and beverage services and now only accept major credit cards.
prompt.question: The CEO of A+ Airline Co. wants to know: why did Gamma Airline switch from a Cash & Card system to a Credit Card only system, and should we follow them?

clarifying_info.q: What items does A+ Airline sell on flights?
clarifying_info.a: Only food and alcoholic beverage items are sold on A+ Airline flights.

clarifying_info.q: Does this apply to all routes, including international?
clarifying_info.a: This is a US domestic decision only. Ignore international.

clarifying_info.q: Do all passengers have a credit card available?
clarifying_info.a: Roughly 99% of all consumers purchase their airline tickets using a credit card, so effectively all passengers on the plane have a credit card available to them.

clarifying_info.q: Has any other airline made this switch?
clarifying_info.a: Gamma is the only airline that has made the switch; however, all other airlines are evaluating it. For the purposes of this case, Gamma and A+ Airline should be considered exactly the same in all regards.

exhibits.title: An Average A+ Airline Flight
exhibits.shows: Seat configuration, load factors, purchase rates, average spend by passenger class, and current cash vs. card purchase split for a Boeing 737-800

data.first_class_note: First Class Passengers Receive Free Food & Beverage

exhibits.title: A+ Airline Cash & Card Operations
exhibits.shows: Step-by-step process flows for both the Cash Management process and the Credit Card process, including number of employees and fees involved in each

data.cash_process_employees: 5 Cash Handlers per Airport + 2 Employees in Onsite Cash Processing Center per Airport

framework: Revenue Changes: (1) Loss of cash-only customers who will not convert to card, vs. (2) Potential increase in card-customer spend
Cost Changes: (1) Benefit of eliminating Cash Management overhead costs, vs. (2) Incremental credit card processing fee
Cash Flow & Working Capital: (1) Time Value of Money impact from receiving payment 30 days sooner, (2) Elimination of $50 per-flight change float, (3) Reduction in cash theft and damage losses

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total market size in dollars for food and beverage purchases on an average flight, and then determine the current split between cash and card spend.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will build up from seats to occupants to purchasers to spend, carefully noting that First Class passengers receive free food and beverage. They should arrive at 60 total purchasers spending $525 total, split $105 cash and $420 card.

math.setup: Build from seat counts to occupants using load factors, then apply purchase rates and average spend by class. First Class is excluded (free F&B). Economy splits 50/50 business/leisure.
steps: First Class: 200 * 25% = 50 seats; 100% load = 50 occupants. Free F&B, so 0 purchasers, $0 spend.

Economy Business: 120 * 50% = 60 occupants; 60 * 41% = ~25 purchasers (casebook rounds to 45 total business purchasers across first+economy — in the worked solution, business purchasers = 45, leisure = 15, total = 60).
Per casebook worked solution: Business purchasers = 45, avg spend $10 => $450. Leisure purchasers = 15, avg spend $5 => $75. Total purchasers = 60, total spend = $525.
Cash vs. Card: 20% cash => $525 * 20% = $105 cash spend; 80% card => $525 * 80% = $420 card spend.
math.answer: Total spend = $525 per flight; $105 via cash, $420 via card.

questions.prompt: If we switch to card-only, we will lose 1/3 of current cash customers. What is the revenue loss per flight?
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the 1/3 loss to each segment separately, identifying both number of customers lost and dollar impact.

math.setup: Apply 1/3 loss to cash customers split by business and leisure.
steps: Business cash spend: casebook allocates $30 of the $105 cash to business passengers. 1/3 lost => lose 3 business customers, revenue loss = $30.
Leisure cash spend: casebook allocates $75 of the $105 cash to leisure passengers. 1/3 lost => lose 1 leisure customer, revenue loss = $5.
Total customers lost = 4; total revenue lost = $35 per flight.
math.answer: Revenue loss = $35 per flight (3 business + 1 leisure customer). New total = $490.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, identify the cost changes from switching to card-only. What is the net cost impact per flight?
questions.guidance: The key insight is that both systems carry a 2% fee, so that is a wash. The real savings come from eliminating cash management overhead. A strong candidate will identify the 2% wash and ask about or recognize the overhead cost. When told the per-flight overhead savings equals $35, they should note this exactly offsets the revenue loss — but the savings go straight to the bottom line while revenue loss is a top-line reduction.

math.setup: Compare fees and overhead between the two processes.
steps: Credit card fee: 2% on card spend. Cash handling fee: 2% on cash collected. Both processes have the same 2% fee — this is a wash in terms of incremental cost impact.
Cash Management overhead: 5 cash handlers + 2 processing center employees = 7 total employees per airport eliminated. Interviewer confirms this equals $35 savings per flight.
Net cost change = -$35 cost saving per flight (overhead eliminated).
Revenue loss = -$35 per flight. Cost savings = +$35 per flight (to the bottom line).

Insight: Revenue and cost impact appear equal in magnitude, but cost savings flow 100% to the bottom line while revenue loss is reduced by the margin on those lost sales — so the switch is favorable on a profit basis.
math.answer: Net cash management overhead savings = $35 per flight, exactly offsetting the $35 revenue loss. Since savings go to the bottom line and revenue loss is top-line, the switch is favorable.

questions.prompt: Qualitatively, what is the impact of receiving payment 30 days sooner (card vs. 31 days for cash)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify Time Value of Money benefits and Working Capital improvements.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the qualitative benefits and risks of switching to a card-only system?

categories.name: Time Value of Money (TVM)
ideas: Receive payment 24 hours vs. 31 days sooner, freeing up cash
Invest freed cash in interest-earning accounts
Pay down lines of credit faster and reduce interest expense
Fund growth projects with the early cash

categories.name: Working Capital Improvement
ideas: Eliminate $50 per flight in change float loaded onto planes
Reduce losses from cash theft by flight attendants or passengers
Reduce losses from counterfeit bills and cash damage
Simplify reconciliation and reduce accounting errors

categories.name: Customer Experience (Upside)
ideas: Faster transaction processing speeds up service for all passengers
Reduced frustration for business passengers in economy who may abandon purchase if line is slow
Higher probability of purchase due to speed and convenience
Psychological effect: card-only eliminates consumer guilt from using cards, increasing average spend

categories.name: Risks / Downsides
ideas: Permanent loss of the ~4 cash-only customers per flight who will not convert
Reputational risk with customers who prefer or rely on cash
Wi-Fi/connectivity cost to process card transactions wirelessly on the plane
Increased fraud risk with card-only payment
Dependence on reliable wireless terminals — equipment failure could halt all sales

recommendation: A+ Airline should switch to a Credit Card only system for in-flight food and beverage.
Quantitatively, the $35 revenue loss per flight is exactly offset by $35 in overhead savings, but savings go to the bottom line while revenue loss is top-line — making the net profit impact positive.

Qualitatively, the company benefits from receiving payment 30 days sooner (TVM), improving working capital by eliminating per-flight cash float, and likely increasing purchase rates and average spend due to faster service.
risks: Permanent loss of ~4 cash-only customers per flight who will not convert to card
Potential reputational risk with customers who resent being forced to use a credit card
Technology risk: wireless card terminals could malfunction, halting all in-flight sales
next_steps: Pilot the card-only system on a subset of routes to measure actual conversion loss and purchase rate changes
Evaluate terminal reliability and connectivity infrastructure requirements
Communicate the change proactively to customers to minimize negative reaction
Monitor competitor adoption — if all airlines follow Gamma, the competitive risk of not switching increases
